title: Pandita Ramabai
hookLine: an Indian scholar and reformer who founded a home for widows and translated the Bible into Marathi

cards: A young woman stands before a hall of learned men in Calcutta, recites long passages of Sanskrit verse from memory, and answers their questions.

They're so impressed they give her titles of honor, and one sticks to her name for life: Pandita, a learned woman. Her father had taught her Sanskrit himself, a gift not every girl of her time was given.
She has walked across much of India with her family. Soon she'll be married, then widowed, with a baby daughter in her arms. What she builds next will be a door for women with nowhere else to go.

teach.h: A WIDOW'S LIFE COULD BE HARD.
teach.b: In the India Ramabai grew up in, a widow's life could be very hard. Some were only girls when their husbands died.
Custom in some families could mean a shaved head, plain clothes, no remarriage, no schooling, and a life at the back of the house. Hindu reformers of her day were working to change this too.
Ramabai knew it from the inside. After her husband's death she traveled to England, and there, among Anglican sisters, she was baptized.
She kept asking questions the whole way and didn't take everything on trust. In America she lectured and raised support.

teach.h: MUKTI: A HOME, AND A SCHOOL.
teach.b: Then she came home and did something practical: she opened a home for widows, where they could live safely and, just as important, learn.

Later she built a larger community on farmland outside Pune and called it Mukti, a word for freedom or deliverance. Women and girls who had been turned away found beds, classrooms, work and dignity there.
Her reason was in the Bible she now read.

The Letter of James puts it bluntly, in the King James Bible: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." Not only feel for them. Visit them.
And in her later years she translated the whole Bible into Marathi, her people's everyday language, working from the Hebrew and Greek herself.
The scholar who once recited Sanskrit to learned men made sure the women of her region could read scripture in the words they spoke at home.

how: The community Ramabai founded near Pune still cares for women and children, and Marathi-speaking Christians remember her as a translator of their Bible.

games.q: you're Ramabai, home in India after your baptism, a widow with a daughter. what do you do first?
o: give lectures in England and stay there.
open a home where widows can live safely and learn.
games.why: she opened a home for widows, a place to live and to learn, and later built Mukti near Pune.

practice: Think of a woman who taught you something: a teacher, a grandmother, a coworker who showed you the ropes. Then think of the women and girls still kept from school today, by money, by custom or by war.
If you pray, pray for one of them; if not, hold her in mind, with thanks for the woman who taught you.
